title: Trees and commits
summary: A tree is a sorted directory listing; a commit is a short text naming a tree and its parents. Rebuild real tree and commit ids byte for byte.

steps.title: Trees
body: A tree object lists one directory. `git cat-file -p` shows it as text:

The **stored** bytes are binary: for each entry, `<mode> <name>\0` followed by the **20 raw bytes** of the id (not 40 hex characters). Entries are sorted by name, where a directory sorts as if its name ended in `/`.
Because a tree holds its children's ids, the root tree's id is a fingerprint of the **whole** snapshot: change any file anywhere and every tree above it gets a new id.

steps.prompt: You change one line in `src/Api/Orders.cs`. Which objects are new in the next commit?
options: A new blob for Orders.cs, new trees for `src/Api`, `src` and the root, and the new commit
Every blob and tree in the project
steps.explain: Ids flow upwards. Unchanged sibling files and folders keep their ids and are simply referenced again, which is why commits are cheap.

steps.prompt: A tree entry for a file is `<mode> <name>\0` plus the raw id bytes. How many bytes is this entry?
steps.explain: `100644` (6) + space (1) + `hello.txt` (9) + NUL (1) = 17, plus 20 raw bytes of SHA-1. A 40-character hex id would have been twice as long.

steps.title: Compute a tree id
prompt: > Conceptual on purpose: real Git builds trees with `git write-tree` (you will use it at the end of this lesson). Writing the byte format once shows why renaming a file changes the tree id but not the blob id.

> Conceptual on purpose: real Git builds trees with `git write-tree` (you will use it at the end of this lesson). Writing the byte format once shows why renaming a file changes the tree id but not the blob id.
Write `TreeId(List<(string Mode, string Name, string Id)> entries)` that returns a real Git tree id:
1. Sort entries by name with `StringComparer.Ordinal`, but compare a directory (mode `40000`) as `name + "/"`.
2. Body = for each entry: UTF-8 bytes of `"<mode> <name>\0"` then `Convert.FromHexString(id)` (20 bytes).
3. Id = SHA-1 of `"tree <body length>\0"` + body, as lowercase hex.
The checks use the real ids of a repo holding `hello.txt` and `src/App.cs`.
starter: static string TreeId(List<(string Mode, string Name, string Id)> entries)
solution: static string TreeId(List<(string Mode, string Name, string Id)> entries)
string Key((string Mode, string Name, string Id) e) => e.Mode == "40000" ? e.Name + "/" : e.Name;
hints: Build the body in a `List<byte>` with `AddRange`.
A local function `Key(e)` returns `e.Name + "/"` for trees, `e.Name` otherwise; pass it to `OrderBy` with `StringComparer.Ordinal`.
The header length is the body's byte count.
template: Dojo.Eq("root: a file and a sub-tree (given out of order)", "a45ecc342b99792adf11582f987b95ee5fcd810e", TreeId(new() { ("40000", "src", "b7b85f87e7da7d7d2944fed5dda605b377f87459"), ("100644", "hello.txt", "ce013625030ba8dba906f756967f9e9ca394464a") }));

steps.title: Commits
body: A commit object is plain text:
- `tree`: the root tree of the snapshot.
- `parent` lines: none for the first commit, one normally, two (or more) for a merge.
- `author` (who wrote the change) and `committer` (who made this commit object), each with a Unix timestamp and time zone. They differ after a rebase or cherry-pick: you become the committer.
- a blank line, then the message (ending with a newline).
Its id is `SHA1("commit <size>\0" + text)`. Since the parent id is part of the text, **a commit's id seals its entire history**: change any ancestor and every descendant's id changes.

steps.prompt: You cherry-pick a teammate's commit. In the new commit, who is the author and who is the committer?
options: Author: your teammate (who wrote the change). Committer: you, with the current time
Author is you, committer is your teammate
steps.explain: Git keeps credit for the change with its author. `git log --format=fuller` shows both.

steps.prompt: Arrange the lines of a commit object with one parent.
steps.explain: Header lines in fixed order (tree, parents, author, committer), a blank line, then the message.

steps.title: Compute a commit id
prompt: > Conceptual on purpose: `git commit-tree` does this for real (next step). Building the text yourself shows why amending only the message still gives a new commit id.
> Conceptual on purpose: `git commit-tree` does this for real (next step). Building the text yourself shows why amending only the message still gives a new commit id.
Write two methods:

- `CommitText(tree, parents, person, time, message)` builds the exact object text: `tree <id>`, one `parent <id>` line per parent, `author <person> <time> +0000`, `committer <person> <time> +0000`, an empty line, then the message, then a final `\n`. Every line ends in `\n`.
- `CommitId(...)` returns SHA-1 of `"commit <byte length>\0" + text` as lowercase hex.
`person` is like `Ada <ada@example.com>`. The checks use ids made by real `git commit-tree`.
starter: static string CommitText(string tree, List<string> parents, string person, long time, string message)
static string CommitId(string tree, List<string> parents, string person, long time, string message)
solution: static string CommitText(string tree, List<string> parents, string person, long time, string message)
static string CommitId(string tree, List<string> parents, string person, long time, string message)
var body = Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(CommitText(tree, parents, person, time, message));
hints: Use a `StringBuilder` and append `\n` explicitly; do not use `AppendLine` (on Windows it adds `\r\n`).
The text ends with the message followed by one `\n`.
Hash exactly like `BlobId`, with `commit` as the type.
template:
Dojo.Eq("first commit text", "tree aaa96ced2d9a1c8e72c56b253a0e2fe78393feb7
author Ada <ada@example.com> 1700000000 +0000
committer Ada <ada@example.com> 1700000000 +0000

Add hello
",
Dojo.Eq("first commit id (git commit-tree)", "b0313dbfea675ba0583498b791d496a6786d5f5f", CommitId("aaa96ced2d9a1c8e72c56b253a0e2fe78393feb7", new(), dojoWho, 1700000000, "Add hello"));

Dojo.Eq("second commit, with a parent", "1b0ca98a4adf40e6313895d1b0500672ee30d710", CommitId("aaa96ced2d9a1c8e72c56b253a0e2fe78393feb7", new() { "b0313dbfea675ba0583498b791d496a6786d5f5f" }, dojoWho, 1700000000, "Second"));

Dojo.Check("changing only the time changes the id", CommitId("aaa96ced2d9a1c8e72c56b253a0e2fe78393feb7", new(), dojoWho, 1700000001, "Add hello") != "b0313dbfea675ba0583498b791d496a6786d5f5f", "ids must differ");

steps.prompt: You amend a commit and change nothing but the message. Which of its ids change? List the ones that change, one per line, from: `tree`, `commit`, `parent`.
steps.explain: The snapshot is identical, so the root tree id is the same, and the parent is the same. The message is part of the commit text, so the commit id changes.

steps.prompt: Match each change to the ids it alters.
pairs: its blob, every tree above it, and the commit
the trees above it and the commit, not the blob
every replayed commit, because their parents change

steps.prompt: Trees sort directories as if their name ended in `/`. What order does this print?
code: var names = new List<(string Name, bool IsDir)> { ("app.cs", false), ("app", true), ("app-tests", true) };
foreach (var n in names.OrderBy(n => n.IsDir ? n.Name + "/" : n.Name, StringComparer.Ordinal))
steps.explain: Compare `app-tests/`, `app.cs` and `app/`: after `app`, the next characters are `-` (45), `.` (46) and `/` (47). Getting this order wrong gives a different, invalid tree id.

steps.title: Make a commit by hand, with plumbing
prompt: Porcelain commands (`add`, `commit`) are built on plumbing. Make a commit in `~/lab` without them:
1. Store a blob for the content `hello` plus a newline: `echo hello | git hash-object -w --stdin`. Compare the id with your C# `BlobId("hello\n")`.
2. Put it in the index as `hello.txt` with `git update-index --add --cacheinfo 100644,<blob>,hello.txt`.
3. Write the index as a tree with `git write-tree`.
4. Make a commit of that tree with the parent `main` and the message `Made by hand`: `git commit-tree`.
5. Point a new branch `plumbing` at it with `git update-ref refs/heads/plumbing <commit>`.
Then look at your work: `git cat-file -p plumbing`, `git ls-tree plumbing`.

checks.name: branch plumbing points at a commit made by hand
checks.cmd: cd ~/lab && test "$(git log -1 --format=%s plumbing)" = 'Made by hand' && test "$(git rev-parse plumbing^)" = "$(cat /opt/dojo/state/main)"
checks.fail: `plumbing` should point at a commit with the message `Made by hand` whose parent is `main`.

checks.name: its tree has hello.txt with the right blob
checks.fail: The commit's tree should list `hello.txt` as blob `ce013625...` (the content `hello` plus a newline).

checks.name: README.md is still in the tree
checks.fail: The tree lost `README.md`. `git write-tree` writes the whole index, which still holds it, so keep using the repo's own index.

hints: Keep the ids in shell variables: `blob=$(echo hello | git hash-object -w --stdin)`.
`c=$(echo 'Made by hand' | git commit-tree $tree -p main)` and `git update-ref refs/heads/plumbing $c`.
solution: c=$(echo 'Made by hand' | git commit-tree "$tree" -p main)
steps.explain: That is all `git commit` does: hash the files into blobs, write the index as a tree, write a commit object pointing at the tree and the parent, and move the branch. Scripts and tools that must never touch your working tree (bots that make commits, `git stash` itself) use exactly these commands. Note that `git status` now shows `hello.txt` as staged on `main`: you changed the index, not a branch.
